title: WavefrontDiffusion: Dynamic Decoding Schedule for Improved Reasoning
claim: Prior schedulers use a global or rigid fixed candidate scope; ours grows the scope dynamically from already-decoded positions.
layout: 3 panels (two stacked left, one tall right), step rows top-to-bottom, shared legend
description: Three rounded boxes compare token-scheduling strategies in diffusion language models. On the left, Standard Diffusion (top) and BlockDiffusion (bottom). On the right, a taller WavefrontDiffusion panel, with a legend box beneath it. Each panel has rows labeled Step = 0, 1, 2, and so on. Each row shows a strip of rounded squares: green for prompt tokens, blue for masks, and purple for completed tokens. A pink arrow leads from each strip to a group of candidate tokens, which are red with a dotted red outline, or dark gray for non-candidates. Standard Diffusion marks every position as a candidate. BlockDiffusion marks a small fixed block, and the block moves only after it is fully denoised. WavefrontDiffusion shows the red candidate window growing outward from the denoised tokens at each step. A caption under each panel states its scope rule. The eye goes first to the red candidate blocks.
caption: Illustration of scheduling strategies in diffusion language models. A Diffusion Language Model predicts all masked tokens. At each step, a scheduling strategy decides which tokens to denoise. There are three strategies: Standard Diffusion uses global scheduling. It always selects tokens from all masked positions. BlockDiffusion limits the choice to a candidate scope. The scope is fixed blocks, similar to semi-autoregression. WavefrontDiffusion also uses a candidate scope. Unlike BlockDiffusion, the scope grows dynamically during decoding.
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have shown strong potential for text generation and are becoming a competitive alternative to autoregressive models. The denoising strategy plays an important role in determining the quality of their outputs. Mainstream denoising strategies include Standard Diffusion and BlockDiffusion. Standard Diffusion performs global denoising without restricting the update range, often finalizing incomplete context and causing premature end-of-sequence predictions. BlockDiffusion updates fixed-size blocks in a preset order, but its rigid structure can break apart coherent semantic units and disrupt reasoning. We present WavefrontDiffusion, a dynamic decoding approach that expands a wavefront of active tokens outward from finalized positions. This adaptive process follows the natural flow of semantic structure while keeping computational cost equal to block-based methods. Across four benchmarks in reasoning and code generation, WavefrontDiffusion achieves state-of-the-art performance while producing outputs with higher semantic fidelity, showing the value of adaptive scheduling for more coherent and efficient generation.
